Scholarly papers tend to end with "more research is required". So does this one, but at least we say so in the headline.

The retraction debate usually arrives as one undifferentiated lump of indignation:  
Fraud, paper mills, AI slop, chatbots citing nonsense.  
It is five problems, owned by five different layers. Fix the wrong layer and you get a very tidy solution to someone else's problem.

## (a) Honest error and correction: The system working

Layer: Authors and editors.

A correction is not a scandal. It’s the scholarly record simply getting on with the job it was supposed to do in the first place.  
The Lancet's first clinical description of COVID-19 patients in Wuhan (Huang et al., 2020, [10.1016/S0140-6736(20)30183-5](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(20)30183-5)) carries an erratum registered in Crossref ([10.1016/s0140-6736(20)30252-x](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0140-6736(20)30252-x)) and is still a perfectly citable paper.  
The failure mode here is not the error - it is a correction that nobody downstream ever sees.

## (b) Misconduct: Fabrication, falsification, authorship abuse

Layer: Institutions and their investigation processes, then editors.

The classics still teach. Obokata's STAP paper in Nature ([10.1038/nature12968](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12968)) was retracted on 2 July 2014 ([notice](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13598)). Hwang's cloned stem-cell paper in Science ([10.1126/science.1094515](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1094515)) got an expression of concern and then a retraction in January 2006 ([notice](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1124926)).  
Authorship abuse is the quieter cousin: In the NIMS case [reported by Retraction Watch](https://x.com/RetractionWatch/status/2112997527402221861), a former supervisor was added as co-author to six papers without permission.  
Our suggestion at the time was cheap: [ask every co-author to confirm authorship and contributor role at submission](https://x.com/DataMercsDotNet/status/2113261868873924890).  
And speed matters: A 2026 Korean parliamentary audit found that 49 of 83 research-misconduct investigations since 2021 took longer than the six months the rules allow (Asia Business Daily, 19 Oct 2026).

## (c) Paper mills: Misconduct with a supply chain

Layer: Publishers' editorial screening, plus collective action.

Paper mills are not one bad scientist. They are an industry, which is why COPE and STM researched them together ([COPE and STM, Paper Mills research report](https://doi.org/10.24318/jtbG8IHL)) and why [United2Act](https://united2act.org/) describes itself as "a growing international movement taking decisive action against the collective challenge of paper mills", adding that "no individual stakeholder can solve this problem alone". Quite. A screening tool at one journal moves the mill to the next journal.

## (d) The plumbing: Retraction status that fails to travel

Layer: Metadata infrastructure, meaning Crossref and [Crossmark](https://www.crossref.org/services/crossmark/), the Retraction Watch database, NISO CREC and PubMed, plus everyone who harvests from them.

This is the layer we care most about, and the one that is easiest to fix. The pieces exist:

- **Crossref** holds update relationships (correction, retraction, expression of concern) that anyone can read in the free REST API. Every retraction cited in this article was checked there, in the `updated-by` field.
- **[Retraction Watch](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/retraction-watch/) data is now public infrastructure.** On 12 September 2023, Crossref [announced](https://doi.org/10.13003/c23rw1d9) that "the Retraction Watch database has been acquired by Crossref and made a public resource", kept populated by Retraction Watch "alongside publishers registering their retraction notices directly with Crossref".
- **NISO RP-45-2024, CREC** ([NISO](https://www.niso.org/standards-committees/crec), approved 26 June 2024) sets out how retractions, removals and expressions of concern should be created, transferred and displayed. Our 21 Oct [reply](https://x.com/DataMercsDotNet/status/2112813147832918244) on a study of 139 Latin American retraction notices ([Publications 14(4):68](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-6775/14/4/68)) noted that "what is affected" and "whether the authors agree" scored lowest.
- **PubMed** links notices and comments to the original record, for example the "Comment on" link we use below.

The pipes leak at the joins. Crossref's own data shows how uneven the labelling is:  
In our test set, the Crossref titles of the  
- *Wakefield* ([10.1016/S0140-6736(97)11096-0](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016%2Fs0140-6736(97)11096-0/transform/application/vnd.crossref.unixsd+xml)),  
- *Surgisphere* ([10.1016/S0140-6736(20)31180-6](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1016%2Fs0140-6736(20)31180-6/transform/application/vnd.crossref.unixsd+xml)),  
- *STAP* ([10.1038/nature12968](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1038%2Fnature12968/transform/application/vnd.crossref.unixsd+xml)),  
- *Boldt* ([10.1093/bja/aen016](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093%2Fbja%2Faen016/transform/application/vnd.crossref.unixsd+xml)) and  
- *Dias* ([10.1038/s41586-023-05742-0](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1038%2Fs41586-023-05742-0/transform/application/vnd.crossref.unixsd+xml))  
papers all start with "RETRACTED", while  
- *Hwang's* ([10.1126/science.1094515](https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1126%2Fscience.1094515/transform/application/vnd.crossref.unixsd+xml)) Science paper, retracted in 2006, does not.  
Title prefixes are human-friendly, but machines should read the relation, not the title.

[ note: check all DOIs for yourself via our *CrossRef DOI checker* here: https://datamercs.net/tools/doi-check/doi-check.html ]

## (e) AI on both sides

Layer: Tool builders and their customers.

AI generates junk at scale, and AI screens and retrieves it. The second half is where honesty helps.  
A Scholarly Kitchen guest post by Sarah Hands ([14 Oct 2026](https://scholarlykitchen.sspnet.org/2026/10/14/guest-post-artificial-intelligence-in-scholarly-publishing-are-we-moving-faster-than-the-evidence/)) put it well:  
"An AI-generated flag isn't necessarily a finding; it is a signal requiring context and interpretation."  
We [quoted it](https://x.com/DataMercsDotNet/status/2113171237241491514) on 22 Oct.

AI search tools inherit whatever retraction metadata they are given. They don't invent the retraction status, and they can't flag what never reached them. NISO's TRACE-supported pilot on a minimum metadata model for AI provenance is the right venue, and [our comment there](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7518485554527731712/) argued that retrieved passages should keep identifier, version, licence, locator and retrieval date. Update status belongs on that list.

## Our anecdote: Four questions in Consensus

Consensus ([consensus.app](https://www.consensus.app)) is a nifty AI search engine for research papers, run by Consensus NLP, Inc., a US company whose terms are governed by Delaware law and which gives a Boston address ([Terms of Service, 25 June 2025](https://consensus.app/home/terms-of-service/)).  
In plain terms: You ask a question in ordinary language, it searches the academic literature, and it answers with a written summary that cites the papers it relied on.  
Its own guide describes it as "an AI search engine for research" that "searches over 400 million scholarly articles" and writes "an answer where every sentence links back to the paper it came from" ([Consensus docs](https://docs.consensus.app/)).

A search runs roughly like this:

1. **The question.** You type something like "Can acid exposure turn ordinary cells into stem cells?"
2. **The search.** Consensus looks through its index. Its abstracts and metadata come from Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and PubMed, and the index is "updated weekly" ([Where the papers come from](https://docs.consensus.app/get-started/where-papers-come-from.md)).
3. **The paper cards.** The papers it found appear as cards with title, authors, year and journal. Inside the answer, small grey tags such as "Seibler 2014" link each statement to its paper, and hovering over one shows the quote it was taken from ([Read a thread](https://docs.consensus.app/learn/read-a-consensus-answer)).
4. **The written answer.** A summary, sometimes with tables, built from those papers.
5. **The Consensus Meter.** For yes-or-no questions, the answer opens with a meter. According to the help centre, the AI "analyzes the top 20 papers returned for your search query" and sorts each paper's conclusion as "Yes", "No", "Possibly" or "Mixed". It needs at least five relevant papers before it shows anything, and every paper it counted is tagged and colour-coded so you can see who voted which way ([The Consensus Meter](https://help.consensus.app/en/articles/10069920-the-consensus-meter)).  
Consensus is candid about the limits: When the meter launched in 2023, the company wrote that its model would "incorrectly classify results 10% of the time" ([Guardrails and Limitations](https://consensus.app/home/blog/consensus-meter/)).

The meter is, in effect, a show of hands among the papers in the room. So it matters a great deal who is let into the room.

On that point, the vendor makes a clear promise. The docs home page says:  
"Retracted papers are flagged and never used in answers."  
For our purposes that sentence carries the whole argument. If a retracted paper is never used, it cannot raise its hand. If it is flagged, a reader who goes looking will know why it is missing.  
Both halves depend on Consensus knowing, from its upstream sources, that a paper has been retracted.

**What we did.** On 23 October we opened a free account and asked one question each about four famous retracted papers:

- **Wakefield et al., The Lancet, 1998**, which suggested a link between the MMR vaccine and autism (10.1016/S0140-6736(97)11096-0). Retracted in February 2010 ([notice](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)60175-4)).
- **Obokata et al., Nature, 2014**, the "STAP" paper, which claimed that a simple acid bath could turn ordinary cells into stem cells. Retracted in July 2014.
- **Hwang et al., Science, 2004**, which claimed human embryonic stem cells from a cloned embryo. Retracted in January 2006.
- **Mehra et al., The Lancet, 2020**, the Surgisphere study, which reported that hydroxychloroquine raised COVID-19 mortality. Retracted in June 2020.

**What we saw.** None of the four retracted papers was cited in any answer. On "never used", Consensus kept its word. On "flagged" we cannot say anything either way, because a paper that never appears cannot show us its flag.

The STAP question was the interesting one. The meter was split: Yes 36, Possibly 18, No 45. Among the papers counted on the yes side were two from 2014, and neither card carried any warning:

- Seibler and Klein, University of Lübeck, in Movement Disorders ([10.1002/mds.25879](https://doi.org/10.1002/mds.25879)), a one-page piece whose title asks whether STAP is "revolutionizing human disease modeling and regenerative therapies?". PubMed classes it as a "Comment" and links it, as "Comment on", to the retracted Nature paper ([PMID 24700468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24700468/)).
- Williams, Xiao, Brownell et al., in Cancer Biology & Therapy ([10.4161/cbt.28414](https://doi.org/10.4161/cbt.28414)), titled "Low pH reprograms somatic murine cells into pluripotent stem cells", classed in PubMed as a "Review" ([PMID 24618709](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24618709/)).

We checked both in Crossref and PubMed. Neither has been retracted or corrected. So, strictly speaking, nothing went wrong: The retracted paper stayed out, as promised. But two cheerful commentaries written in the few months when STAP still looked like a revolution were let in, and each was counted as a "yes" vote for a finding the world withdrew in July 2014. A reader glancing at the meter would see a third of the room saying "yes", and no card telling them why that third should be taken with a pinch of salt.

**The gap.** The records already know both facts: PubMed knows that the Lübeck piece is a “comment on” the Nature paper, and Crossref knows that the Nature paper is retracted. Yet, no one joins the two and sends the result one step further down the pipe:  
"This paper comments on a retracted paper."  
That is not a failing peculiar to Consensus. It is the plumbing problem from section (d), only this time it’s coming out of a different tap. It is also cheap to fix, because both facts are already in open metadata.

**Why four questions is an anecdote.** Four questions, one tool, one free account, one afternoon.  
We chose famous cases, which a well-built system is most likely to handle. We did not repeat the questions, try other wordings, compare other tools or test the paid research agent. Answers change as the index updates weekly. And our meter figures come from a single screenshot. It shows how one failure can happen. It doesn't tell us how often it does. For that we have written a fuller [test plan](https://www.datamercs.net/posts/2026-10-23-retractions-ai-plumbing/consensus-test-plan_PUBLIC.md): 12 papers with checked ground truth, four ways of asking, and a scoring rubric. *More research required*, just as promised.

## Homework

**Librarians and discovery teams**
1. Check whether your discovery layer and link resolver read Crossref update relations, or only titles.
2. Spot-check five famous retractions in your catalogue: Is the notice linked, and is the original labelled?
3. Ask every AI search vendor the five questions below before the next renewal.

**Publishers**
1. Register every correction, retraction and expression of concern as a Crossref update, with the notice as its own DOI. Follow CREC for wording and display.
2. Put "what is affected" and "whether the authors agree" in every notice template.
3. Confirm authorship and CRediT roles with every co-author at submission, not only the corresponding author.

**Metadata people and tool builders**
1. Harvest `updated-by` and re-harvest on a schedule, using Crossref's `from-update-date` filter.
2. Propagate one hop: Flag "comments on" and "replies to" retracted works, and say why.
3. Carry update status in AI provenance payloads, next to identifier and version.

**Vendor questions**
1. Which sources set your retraction flag, and how quickly?
2. Do you track corrections and expressions of concern, or only retractions?
3. Is update status exposed in the API?
4. Do you flag papers that cite or comment on retracted work as support?
5. How do you pair preprints with versions of record?

## Verdict

The fix is better metadata, not refusing to use AI. Use the machines, but feed them the whole record.  
The rest, naturally, *requires more research*.
